# CLOSING

## Three corrections worth remembering

These are places where reasonable inference gives the wrong answer, which makes them the places you are most likely to be wrong too.

**Evaluation sets should be large and automatically graded, not small and hand-curated.** The instinct that a carefully curated small set beats a big rough one is wrong as stated. Task-specificity governs what goes in, but when the choice is many automated cases against few manual ones, take the many. Human grading does not scale, and a set that cannot be run on every change is a set that will not be run.

**"Too many tools" has two different answers and they are not interchangeable.** If the role does not need the capability, remove it, and no loading strategy fixes the security exposure. If the catalog is legitimately large and every tool is appropriate to the role, removal is unavailable and the answer is to defer the definitions. Diagnosing which problem you have is the whole of the work; the remedy follows.

**Your own instructions do not belong in tool results.** The channel that makes third-party content safe is the same channel that makes your instructions unreliable, because the model is trained to distrust it. This inverts the natural instinct to attach an instruction to the content it concerns.

## The stance

Nearly half of this material is about things that are not code: governance, risk, compliance, discovery, trade-off communication, documentation, handoff and the end of a system's life. That is not the soft part of the discipline. It is the part that describes what an architect actually is, and it is the part where a career spent making consequential decisions under constraint counts for more than any amount of product recall.

The single highest-yield habit in the whole document is the one the Practice Layer is built around. Given a system, ask what is wrong with it in a fixed order, and let each question rule out the work you would otherwise do next. Most expensive pivots are not failures of skill. They are decisions taken in the wrong order by people who never wrote the order down.

Final Liability rests with the Human.
